summary:
Nunavut is a territory of Canada and stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework of the country. The territory's own Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression: members of the Legislative Assembly voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31 on 13 March 2017, and Justice Minister Keith Peterson stated that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited.

On 18 September 2025 Nunavut members of the Legislative Assembly voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore a third, non-binary sex designation on Nunavut birth certificates through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck the option from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill. The bill was then approved on third reading. Sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut "now joins the rest of Canada in recognizing non-binary and transgender individuals".

Since 22 March 2022 the Nunavut Health Department has funded transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty among the procedures named, delivered under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The territorial LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside the territorial capital.

The inventory contains no documented incident of violence against a trans person in Nunavut, no dated case with an outcome, and no territorial enforcement record under the 2017 amendment. The most recent Nunavut-specific development in this record is the birth-certificate vote of 18 September 2025; no later instance is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Statistics Canada's release "Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024" (published 30 March 2026) records 4,882 police-reported hate crimes nationally, up 1% over the year and 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and 184% above 2020; sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, with June 2024 alone recording 113 against a monthly average near 50. The release gives no Nunavut breakdown and reports rates roughly 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a distinction Nunavut does not present, since it has no metropolitan reporting hub of that kind.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an NGO reading of the same police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations, likewise supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than any territorial figure.

At the passage of Bill 31 in March 2017, nine provinces and one territory listed gender identity or expression in their human-rights laws, which made Nunavut the first Canadian territory to do so.

A 2020 poll commissioned by the Privy Council Office found 87.6% of respondents said they would be "comfortable" if a neighbour was a transgender person, against 91.8% who said the same of a gay, lesbian or bisexual neighbour; this is a national attitudinal figure, not a Nunavut measure.
localsOnly:
Nunavut residents can request the non-binary sex designation on territorial birth certificates following the amendments to the Vital Statistics Act approved in September 2025, after the option had earlier been struck from the bill in committee.

Transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents has been funded by the Nunavut Health Department since 22 March 2022, covering the named procedures of breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty through the partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal.

Positive Space, the territorial LGBTQ group, reported in March 2022 that residents living outside the territorial capital face information gaps in reaching that care, a disparity the sources do not quantify.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Nunavut-specific hate-crime or violence statistic appears anywhere in the inventory. The Statistics Canada release reports nationally and by metropolitan area without identifying Nunavut, so no territorial rate can be stated and none is inferred here.

The inventory contains no account of a human-rights complaint brought under the Nunavut Human Rights Act, no complaint outcome, and no record of how the 2017 amendment has been enforced.

Whether a visitor or newcomer to Nunavut can reach the territorially funded transition-care programme is unresolved: the sources describe the funding as directed at residents and do not state eligibility rules, waiting lists or costs for someone without resident status.

No source in the inventory addresses screening at the territorial airport or any border entry point, document-marker checks on arrival, or facilities access for trans travellers in Nunavut.

Material in the inventory on national statutes, other Canadian provinces' legislation and nationwide attitudinal surveys is not specific to Nunavut and is not carried in this record.
